theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes workplace mentoring?
options: A manager checking each day that a new worker follows the rules and procedures
A longer-term relationship in which an experienced person guides another's growth
A short course run by an outside trainer on a single technical skill for staff
A meeting at which each worker's pay is reviewed against the market rate every year

questions.stem: How does mentoring usually differ from coaching?
options: Mentoring is always paid for by the employee, while coaching is free to staff
Mentoring deals only with technical skills, while coaching deals only with feelings
Mentoring is broader and longer-term; coaching usually targets set skills or goals
Mentoring is done in groups of twenty, while coaching is always one to one

questions.stem: Why do many organisations avoid making a person's line manager their mentor?
options: Because line managers are never experienced enough to guide their staff
Because the law forbids managers from giving advice to their own staff
Because line managers would then have to give up their own management work
Because the mentee may not speak openly to someone who appraises them

questions.stem: A Kingston hotel starts mentoring for new supervisors. Which benefit to the hotel is most likely?
options: New supervisors settle faster and are more likely to stay
The hotel no longer needs any formal training for supervisors
The hotel can stop all appraisals of its supervisors
Supervisors no longer need any contact with their own managers

questions.stem: What does a mentor usually gain from mentoring?
options: A guaranteed promotion at the end of the agreed mentoring period, in writing
Better listening and leadership skills, and fresh views on the work
Authority to give the mentee instructions about daily tasks
An extra payment from the mentee for each meeting held

questions.stem: Which quality matters most in a workplace mentor?
options: Being the most senior person available in the organisation
Having exactly the same background and interests as the mentee
Being trustworthy, a good listener and willing to give time
Being able to solve every problem for the mentee quickly

questions.stem: A school is matching mentors with newly qualified teachers. Which approach is best?
options: Pair each new teacher with whoever has the most free periods this term
Let senior staff choose the new teachers they like best on the first day
Pair each new teacher with the head of their own department in every single case
Match on the mentee's needs and goals, the mentor's skills and both people's views

questions.stem: Tamara Reid has agreed to mentor a new procurement officer in a ministry. What should she do before their first meeting?
options: Learn about the mentee's role and the scheme's aims, and plan the first meeting
Write a full set of goals for the mentee to accept at the first meeting
Read the mentee's full personal file, including his medical and pay records
Ask the mentee's colleagues for their honest opinion of him

questions.stem: What is the main aim of the first mentoring meeting?
options: To solve the mentee's most urgent work problem in full before they part
To build rapport and agree how the relationship will work
To assess the mentee's performance for the appraisal
To tell the mentee the mentor's full career history

questions.stem: Which item belongs in a mentoring agreement?
options: The mentee's salary and the mentor's salary, for comparison
A promise that the mentee will be promoted within one year
Goals, how often to meet, confidentiality and how to end it
A list of the mentee's past mistakes at work

questions.stem: A mentee tells his mentor in confidence that he is struggling with his workload. When may the mentor share this without his agreement?
options: Whenever the mentee's manager asks about him
When the mentor thinks it would make an interesting example in training
At the end of the mentoring relationship, in a report to HR
Only where there is a serious risk of harm, as the agreement sets out

questions.stem: Why should the limits of confidentiality be explained at the start of the relationship?
options: So the mentee knows what will stay private and when it might not
So the mentor can share the meeting notes with the mentee's manager freely
So that the mentee can be disciplined for what they say
So that the relationship can be ended without notice

questions.stem: A mentee says her goal is 'to get better at my job'. What should the mentor help her do?
options: Accept the goal as it is, so as not to discourage her
Make it specific, measurable and time-bound, such as a SMART goal
Choose a different goal for her, one that the mentor prefers and knows well
Drop goal-setting and simply meet when she has problems

questions.stem: A mentee drafts four goals. Which one meets all the SMART tests?
options: Improve my communication skills in general over the coming year
Become a much better manager than I am now
Lead two team briefings a month and get feedback by March
Try to be more confident whenever I can

questions.stem: How can a mentor best help a mentee find out what she needs to learn?
options: Tell her what she needs, based on the mentor's own first job
Ask her manager for her appraisal ratings and use only those
Give her a list of courses and ask her to pick three
Use questions, self-assessment and feedback to explore her strengths and gaps

questions.stem: A mentor structures a conversation as Goal, Reality, Options and Way forward. What is this model called?
options: GROW
SWOT
SMART
PESTLE

questions.stem: During a mentoring meeting, which action by the mentor best shows that she is truly listening?
options: Planning the next point while the mentee is still talking
Summarising what the mentee said and checking it is right
Looking at the phone to show how busy the mentor is
Finishing the mentee's sentences to save time

questions.stem: Which question is open and helps the mentee think for herself?
options: Did you finish the report on time?
Was the meeting with the client a success?
What could you do differently next time?
Do you agree that you should have asked first?

questions.stem: A mentee asks, 'What should I do about my difficult supervisor?' What is usually the best first response?
options: Tell him exactly what you would do in his place
Tell him to ignore the problem and it will go away
Offer to speak to the supervisor on his behalf
Ask what has happened and what options he can see

questions.stem: A mentor watched her mentee present to a client. Which feedback is most helpful?
options: Your opening grabbed attention; slow down on the figures so the client can follow
That was fine, well done, and there is really nothing much to add
You were nervous, which everyone could see from the start
You should present the way I did when I was in your job, as that worked for me

questions.stem: When is it most useful for a mentor to share a story from her own career?
options: At the start of every meeting, to fill the time
When it helps the mentee see options, not to tell him what to do
Whenever the mentee mentions a problem, before he finishes
Only when the story shows how successful the mentor is

questions.stem: Why does a mentor ask the mentee to reflect on what happened after a new task?
options: So that the mentor can report the mistakes to the mentee's manager afterwards
So that the mentee feels guilty about what went wrong
So that the mentee learns from experience and plans the next step
So that the mentoring meeting lasts for the full hour

questions.stem: What most helps trust grow between a mentor and mentee?
options: Meeting only when the mentor has free time
Keeping all meetings very short and formal
Avoiding any talk of the mentee's goals
Keeping promises, being honest and respecting confidentiality

questions.stem: In a common model, mentoring moves through stages: starting, building, separating and redefining. What usually happens in the 'separating' stage?
options: The mentee becomes more independent and the formal relationship winds down
The mentor and mentee meet for the very first time and get to know each other
The mentor and mentee agree their first goals
The mentor takes over the mentee's work

questions.stem: A mentee begins to share serious personal and family problems at every meeting. What should the mentor do?
options: Act as the mentee's counsellor and meet more often
Listen with care, and point her to the employee assistance programme or other help
Tell the mentee's manager so that work can be reduced
End the relationship at once without explanation

questions.stem: A mentee asks his mentor, a senior manager, to make sure he is shortlisted for a promotion. What should the mentor do?
options: Agree, as helping the mentee's career is the mentor's main job in the scheme
Speak privately to the interview panel on his behalf
Explain that she cannot influence the selection, but can help him prepare
Tell the mentee not to apply this year

questions.stem: A mentee now asks her mentor before making even small decisions. What should the mentor do?
options: Keep answering every question so the mentee does not feel let down
Make the decisions for her until the end of the relationship
Stop replying to her messages without warning
Encourage her to think through options first and build her confidence

questions.stem: A mentee keeps cancelling mentoring meetings at short notice. What should the mentor do first?
options: Talk openly with the mentee about what is getting in the way
Report the mentee to her manager for a poor attitude to the mentoring scheme
End the relationship without discussing it
Carry on as normal and say nothing

questions.stem: A mentor in an agency is 30 years older than her mentee and grew up in a different parish and culture. What is the best approach?
options: Expect the mentee to adopt the mentor's own ways of working and thinking
Stay open, ask about the mentee's views and avoid assumptions
Avoid any talk about background or values
Ask for a mentee of the same age

questions.stem: A young staff member helps a senior director learn to use new digital tools. What is this arrangement called?
options: Group mentoring
Line management
Reverse mentoring
Formal appraisal

questions.stem: Officers in Negril and Port Antonio are mentored by a manager in Kingston through video calls and messages. What should the mentor pay special attention to?
options: Making every call as long as possible
Sending feedback only by email so it is recorded
Cancelling calls whenever the internet is slow
Agreeing a regular schedule and keeping calls private and secure

questions.stem: Why is a mentor's own behaviour at work important to the mentoring?
options: Because mentees often learn as much from what mentors do as from what they say
Because the mentor's conduct is graded by the mentee
Because the mentor is paid according to her behaviour
Because the mentee must copy everything the mentor does

questions.stem: What kind of notes should a mentor keep after each meeting?
options: A word-for-word record of everything the mentee says during each meeting
Brief notes of goals, agreed actions and progress, kept securely
Notes on the mentee's private life for the HR file
No notes at all, so that nothing is ever written down

questions.stem: Three months into mentoring, what should the mentor and mentee do?
options: Start completely new goals without looking back at the ones already agreed
Ask the mentee's manager to judge the mentor
Review progress on the goals and how the relationship is working
Meet less often whether the goals are met or not

questions.stem: A mentor and mentee meet once a month for 1.5 hours over a year. How much meeting time is that?
options: 12 hours
15 hours
24 hours
18 hours

questions.stem: The mentee has met her goals and the agreed period is over. How should the formal relationship end?
options: With a closing meeting to review learning and agree next steps
By the mentor no longer replying to messages
By HR sending a letter with no meeting
By the mentee finding a new mentor without telling the first one or anyone else

questions.stem: The relationship is not working: the mentee and mentor clash on every point. What is the best step?
options: Keep meeting until the agreed year is over
Talk honestly, and agree a no-fault end and a possible new match
Let the relationship lapse quietly without saying anything to the mentee about it
Report the mentee to HR for being difficult

questions.stem: A mentor learns that her mentee is planning to leave for a rival firm. What should she do?
options: Tell the mentee's manager at once so that they can take steps to stop her
Try to persuade her to stay by promising a pay rise
Respect the confidence and help her think through the choice
End the mentoring because she is leaving

questions.stem: A mentor's comments to a mentee become personal and unwelcome. What principle has been broken?
options: The need for SMART goals
The need to meet monthly
The need to keep notes
Respect, and a safe relationship free of harassment

questions.stem: How can a mentor keep improving her mentoring skills?
options: Ask for feedback, reflect, and talk with other mentors or the scheme lead
Mentor as many people as possible at the same time
Use the same approach with every mentee
Avoid training, as experience is enough

questions.stem: A parish council plans a mentoring scheme for new officers. Which step should come first?
options: Choose the mentors from the most senior staff in each department of the council
Agree the scheme's purpose and how success will be measured
Book a launch event at a hotel
Order mentoring workbooks for every officer

questions.stem: Why should new mentors receive training before the scheme starts?
options: So that they can supervise the mentees' daily work as well as mentor them
So that the scheme can avoid having a coordinator
So they understand the role, its limits and key skills
So that they can mentor without an agreement

questions.stem: Of 20 new staff who had mentors, 18 were still employed after a year. What is the retention rate?
Which evidence best shows whether a mentoring scheme is working?
options: Goal progress, feedback from both sides, and retention compared with before
The number of mentoring meetings booked in the calendar
The cost of the launch event
How long each mentor has worked for the firm

questions.stem: A mentee says she has felt hopeless for weeks and sometimes thinks of harming herself. What should the mentor do?
options: Promise to keep it secret and change the subject
Take it seriously, stay with her and get urgent help, as the agreement allows
Tell her to take a few days off and see how she feels
Suggest they talk about it at next month's meeting

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the person who receives guidance in a mentoring relationship usually called?
What four-letter name is given to the model Goal, Reality, Options, Way forward?
In the SMART test for goals, what does the letter 'T' usually stand for? (One or two words.)
What two-word term names the written understanding of goals, meetings, confidentiality and ending that mentor and mentee sign?
When a mentor repeats the mentee's main points in her own words to check she has understood, what one-word skill is she using?
What two-word term names mentoring in which a junior person guides a senior one, for example on digital tools?
What two-word term names mentoring between colleagues at about the same level?
What one-word term names the feeling of mutual trust and understanding that lets mentor and mentee talk openly?
What kind of question, such as 'What options do you see?', cannot be answered with just yes or no? (One word, before 'question'.)
What one-word term names the limits a mentor keeps, such as not acting as the mentee's counsellor or manager?
A mentor and mentee meet every two weeks for 1 hour over 6 months. About how many hours of meetings is that?
Of 25 mentees, 22 met all their agreed goals. What percentage met their goals?
What term names mentoring carried out mainly by email, messages and video calls? (Hyphenated or two words.)
What one-word term names thinking back over an experience to learn from it and plan what to do next?
In the four-stage model (initiation, cultivation, separation, redefinition), which stage comes after cultivation?

essays.stem: Compare mentoring, coaching and line management, and explain when each is the best way to support a new supervisor.
essays.modelAnswer: Line management is the formal relationship in which a manager sets work, checks results and appraises performance. It is the right route for day-to-day direction, standards and decisions about the supervisor's job. Coaching is usually shorter and focused: a coach, often the manager or a trained colleague, helps the person improve a set skill or reach a set goal, such as running team briefings, mainly through questions and practice. It suits a clear skill gap. Mentoring is broader and longer-term. An experienced person outside the line, who does not appraise the mentee, helps her settle, understand the organisation's culture, build confidence and plan her career, drawing on experience and asking questions. Because it is confidential and separate from appraisal, she can admit doubts openly. For a new supervisor I would use all three: line management for duties and standards, coaching for the specific skills she lacks, and a mentor from another department to support her growth and confidence over the first year.
markingPoints: Line management: direction, standards and appraisal
Coaching: focused, shorter, skill or goal based
Mentoring: broader, longer, outside the line, confidential
Explains when each is the best choice
Recommends a sensible combination for the new supervisor

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan and run the first meeting with a new mentee.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the meeting I would read about the scheme's aims and the mentee's role, and choose a quiet, private place and enough time, about an hour. I would start by introducing myself briefly and inviting the mentee to tell me about herself, her work so far and what she hopes to gain, listening carefully and asking open questions to build rapport. I would explain what mentoring is and is not: I will listen, ask questions, share experience and give honest feedback, but I am not her manager, will not appraise her and cannot secure promotions. Together we would draft a mentoring agreement: two or three broad goals to refine later, how often and where we meet, how to contact each other, what stays confidential and its limits, such as a serious risk of harm, and how either of us can end the relationship. I would end by summarising what we agreed, setting one small action for each of us and fixing the next date, then send a short note confirming it.
markingPoints: Prepares: learns about the role and scheme, chooses a private setting
Builds rapport with open questions and listening
Explains the mentor's role and its limits
Agrees goals, meetings, contact, confidentiality and ending
Summarises, sets actions and the next date, confirms in writing

essays.stem: Explain why confidentiality matters in mentoring, what its limits are, and how a mentor should handle a situation where it may have to be broken.
essays.modelAnswer: Confidentiality matters because mentoring works only if the mentee can speak openly about doubts, mistakes and ambitions without fear that they will reach her manager or colleagues. Without it, she will say only safe things and learn little. Confidentiality is not absolute. The limits should be agreed at the start and written into the mentoring agreement. They usually include a serious risk of harm to the mentee or others, a disclosure of a crime or of serious wrongdoing such as fraud, and anything the law or the organisation's policy requires to be reported, such as harassment or a safety danger. If such a matter arises, the mentor should listen calmly, remind the mentee of the agreed limits, and explain what she needs to do and why. Where possible, she should encourage the mentee to report it herself and offer support. She should share only what is necessary, only with the right person, such as the scheme lead, HR or emergency help, and keep a brief, secure note of what she did.
markingPoints: Explains why confidentiality is essential to open, useful mentoring
Limits are agreed at the start and written down
Names typical limits: risk of harm, crime or serious wrongdoing, legal duties
Handles a breach: reminds of limits, explains, encourages self-reporting
Shares only what is needed with the right person and records it

essays.stem: A mentee says she wants to 'move into management one day'. Explain how you would help her turn this into a mentoring plan.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by exploring what she means: which kind of management role, why she wants it and by when. Using the GROW model, I would ask about her goal, then her reality: what experience and skills she has now, and what feedback she has had. I might ask her to rate herself against the main skills in a supervisor's job description, such as leading people, planning, budgets and communication, and to seek feedback from a colleague. Together we would pick two or three gaps that matter most. I would then help her write SMART goals, for example: 'Lead my team's weekly briefing for three months and get feedback from my manager by June' or 'Complete a short budgeting course by September'. For each goal we would agree actions, the support she needs, such as shadowing a manager, and how we will know it is done. The plan would be written, kept by her, and reviewed every two or three months, with goals changed as she grows.
markingPoints: Explores the meaning and timing of the ambition
Uses a structure such as GROW to examine the present position
Uses self-assessment and feedback to find key gaps
Writes SMART goals with actions and support
Records the plan and reviews it regularly

essays.stem: Evaluate the skills a mentor needs, and explain how each one helps the mentee.
essays.modelAnswer: Active listening is the most important skill: giving full attention, summarising and checking understanding shows respect and helps the mentee clarify her own thinking. Questioning, especially open questions such as 'What options do you see?', helps her solve problems for herself rather than depend on the mentor. Giving feedback that is specific, balanced and timely helps her see what to repeat and what to change, without damaging confidence. Sharing experience is useful when it widens her view of options, but if overused it becomes telling and limits her growth. Building rapport and trust, through reliability and confidentiality, makes honest conversations possible. Goal-setting and planning skills turn good conversations into action. Self-awareness and cultural sensitivity help the mentor avoid assuming that what worked for her will suit a mentee of a different age, background or role. Overall, the skills that encourage independence, listening and questioning, matter most, because the aim is for the mentee to grow, not to rely on the mentor.
markingPoints: Active listening and why it helps
Open questioning that builds independence
Specific, balanced feedback
Sharing experience used carefully; rapport, trust and goal-setting
Evaluates which skills matter most and why

essays.stem: Describe the boundaries a mentor should keep, and how she should respond when a mentee pushes against them.
essays.modelAnswer: A mentor should keep several boundaries. She is not the mentee's manager, so she does not direct his work or report on his performance. She is not a counsellor or therapist, so serious personal or health problems should be referred to the employee assistance programme or professional help. She cannot use her position to influence promotions, selections or discipline. She should keep the relationship professional, with agreed times and ways of contact, and avoid financial dealings or favours. When a mentee pushes against a boundary, for example by asking her to speak to the interview panel for him, she should respond calmly and kindly, explain the boundary and why it protects both of them and the scheme, and offer what she can do instead, such as helping him prepare for the interview. If the mentee repeatedly brings personal crises, she should show care, point to the right help and refocus meetings on the agreed goals. If a boundary problem continues, she should discuss it openly and, if needed, seek advice from the scheme lead.
markingPoints: Not a manager: no directing work or reporting performance
Not a counsellor: refers serious personal issues to proper help
No influence on selection or discipline; professional contact only
Responds calmly, explains the boundary and offers an alternative
Refocuses meetings and seeks advice from the scheme lead if problems continue

essays.stem: Four months into a mentoring relationship, the mentee seems to rely on you for every decision. Explain why this is a problem and plan how you would deal with it.
essays.modelAnswer: Dependency is a problem because the purpose of mentoring is to build the mentee's own judgement and confidence. If she checks every decision with me, she learns less, may look unsure to her manager and colleagues, and could struggle when the relationship ends. It also takes more of my time than we agreed. I would first reflect on my own part: have I been giving answers too quickly instead of asking questions? At our next meeting I would raise it openly and kindly, praising her progress and explaining that I want to help her trust her own judgement. We would agree some changes: she brings her own options and a preferred choice before asking my view; she makes small decisions on her own and reflects on them with me later; and contact between meetings is for urgent matters only. I would use more open questions, such as 'What would you advise someone else to do?', and recognise good decisions she makes. We would review this in a month.
markingPoints: Explains why dependency harms the mentee and the relationship
Reflects on the mentor's own part in it
Raises it openly and supportively
Agrees practical changes that build independence
Uses questioning and recognition, and reviews progress

essays.stem: Plan a mentoring scheme for newly appointed officers in a public agency with offices in three parishes.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first agree the purpose with senior management: to help new officers settle quickly, understand public service values and stay with the agency, with measures such as retention after one year and officers' feedback. I would name a scheme coordinator. Mentors would be volunteers with at least three years' service and good references, outside the mentee's line, and would receive a half-day training session on the role, boundaries, confidentiality, GROW and feedback. Matching would use a short form from each mentee and mentor, considering goals, skills and location, with the option of video calls between parishes. Each pair would sign a mentoring agreement and meet about monthly for twelve months. I would provide simple guides and review forms, and hold a check-in with mentors every quarter to share lessons and deal with problems. The scheme would include a no-fault way to end a pair that does not work. At the end of the year I would gather goal progress, feedback and retention figures and report the results with recommendations.
markingPoints: Agrees purpose and measures of success with management, and names a coordinator
Selects and trains mentors, outside the line
Matches pairs sensibly, including distance arrangements
Sets agreements, meeting pattern, guides and ongoing support for mentors
Includes a no-fault exit and evaluates the scheme at the end

essays.stem: Explain how differences in age, gender, culture or background can affect a mentoring relationship, and how a mentor should handle them.
essays.modelAnswer: Differences can enrich mentoring, because each person brings new views, but they can also cause misunderstanding. A mentor much older than the mentee may assume that the career paths of the past still apply, while a young mentee may hesitate to disagree with an elder. Gender can affect how comfortable a mentee feels raising some issues, and both must take care that the relationship stays professional. Cultural and regional backgrounds, such as growing up in a rural parish or a city, or different religious practices, can shape communication styles, attitudes to authority and expectations about work and family. Disability may require changes to meeting places or methods. A mentor should handle these by staying curious and open, asking rather than assuming, listening to the mentee's experience and being aware of her own biases. She should adapt her style, for example being more direct or more patient, and arrange meetings that suit the mentee's needs. If either person feels the match is not working, a respectful change should be possible.
markingPoints: Recognises that differences can both enrich and complicate mentoring
Gives examples for age and gender
Gives examples for culture, background or disability
Handles differences by curiosity, listening and awareness of own bias
Adapts style and arrangements, and allows a respectful change of match

essays.stem: A hotel has run a mentoring scheme for new supervisors for one year. Of 20 mentees, 18 are still employed, compared with 14 of 20 supervisors hired the year before without mentors. Evaluate the scheme and recommend what to do next.
essays.modelAnswer: Retention was 18 ÷ 20 = 90% for the mentored group, against 14 ÷ 20 = 70% for the year before, a rise of 20 percentage points. This suggests the scheme helps, but it does not prove it, because other things may have changed, such as pay, the labour market or a new general manager. I would look for more evidence. I would check how many mentees met their agreed goals, ask mentees and their managers whether skills and confidence improved, and ask mentors what worked and what did not. I would look at how often pairs met, since pairs that seldom met may have gained little, and at any relationships that ended early. I would also weigh the costs: mentors' time, training and coordination. If the extra evidence supports the result, I recommend continuing the scheme, training more mentors, fixing weaknesses found, such as irregular meetings, and keeping a comparison group or a before-and-after measure so that next year's evaluation is stronger.
markingPoints: Works out 90% and 70% retention correctly
Notes that other factors may explain the change
Gathers further evidence: goals, feedback, meeting records
Weighs costs against benefits
Recommends next steps, including improvements and better evaluation

practical1.title: Set up a mentoring relationship: first meeting role play and mentoring agreement
practical1.brief: Your group practises starting a mentoring relationship in a workplace chosen from the assessor's cards (for example, a hotel front office, a school office or a government agency). Form two pairs: in each, one member is the mentor and one the mentee, and in the second half the pairs swap roles so that every member is mentor once. The fifth member (or the assessor in a group of four) is the observer, using an observation sheet. Each mentor runs a 20-minute first meeting: builds rapport, explains the role and its limits, agrees confidentiality and its limits, and drafts with the mentee a written mentoring agreement and two SMART goals. After each meeting the observer and the mentee give feedback, and the mentor writes a short reflection on what went well and what to improve. Each member's mentoring agreement, goals and reflection are handed in, with the observer's sheets. The mentee's story must be made up, not a real personal problem.
materials: Workplace scenario cards and made-up mentee profiles from the assessor
SMART goal sheet and observation sheet
A quiet space with chairs for each pair, and a timer
photos: Each pair seated for the first meeting (no faces needed: hands and papers are enough)
checklist: As mentor, built rapport using open questions and active listening
Explained the mentor's role and its limits clearly
Agreed confidentiality and its limits in plain words
Helped the mentee write two goals that meet the SMART test
Completed a mentoring agreement covering goals, meetings, contact and ending
Wrote an honest reflection with one clear improvement
safety: Use only the made-up mentee profiles; do not share real personal problems
Keep observation sheets and reflections confidential to the group and the assessor
Any member may pause the role play if it becomes uncomfortable
Give feedback on behaviour, not on the person

practical2.title: Design a workplace mentoring scheme and present it to management
practical2.brief: Your group has been asked by the general manager of a hotel group (or the head of a public agency, as the assessor chooses) to design a one-year mentoring scheme for new supervisors. Produce: (1) a one-page scheme outline (purpose, who takes part, how mentors are chosen and matched, meeting pattern and support); (2) mentor guidelines on the role, boundaries and confidentiality; (3) a one-page outline of a half-day mentor training session; (4) a progress review form; and (5) an evaluation plan with measures, such as goal completion and retention, and a worked example of how retention will be calculated. Give each member a named role: scheme lead (outline and checking), guidelines writer, training designer, forms and records officer, and in a group of five an evaluation officer. Present the scheme to the assessor as the general manager, in a 15-minute presentation with slides or a poster, each member presenting their part. Photograph each stage.
materials: Computer with word processor and presentation software, or flipchart paper and markers
photos: The planning sheet with each member's name and role
The scheme outline and the mentor guidelines
The training session outline and the progress review form
The evaluation plan with the worked retention example
The group presenting the scheme to the assessor
checklist: Carried out a named role and produced their own part of the evidence
Scheme outline states a clear purpose, matching method and meeting pattern
Guidelines set out the mentor's role, boundaries and confidentiality limits correctly
Training outline covers key skills such as listening, questioning, feedback and goal-setting
Evaluation plan has sensible measures and a correct worked example
Presented their part clearly and answered questions
Worked respectfully with the group and shared the workload
safety: Use made-up names and figures only
Make sure the guidelines tell mentors to refer serious personal problems to proper help
Keep the scheme design respectful of all ages, genders and backgrounds
Take a short screen break each hour
